section_summary: This section traces U.S. dealings with Japanese passport, visa, landing, residence, and transit rules from 1930 through 1939. It includes a major report on Japan’s state-supported tourist industry; cases involving travelers, entertainers, naval personnel, Chinese residents of Taiwan, and German Jews; and the full translation of Japan’s new 1939 alien-entry ordinance. Cross-reference sheets also point to related complaints about fees, detention, discriminatory treatment, and refusals of permission to land.

subfiles.title: Telegram asking where Japanese, Korean, and Manchurian visas may be obtained
subfiles.about: Huston asks whether visas for Japan, Korea, and Manchuria can be obtained in Los Angeles or Seattle.
subfiles.summary: Telegram from Blanchard, Iowa, asks the Passport Division which West Coast city could issue Japanese, Korean and Manchurian visas.

subfiles.title: Reply identifying Japanese consulates in Los Angeles and Seattle
subfiles.from: Ruth B. Shipley, Chief, Passport Division
subfiles.about: The Passport Division advises that Japanese consuls are located in both Los Angeles and Seattle.
subfiles.summary: The Department answers the inquiry of August 28. Its brief response identifies both cities as locations of Japanese consular offices.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Voluntary Report No. 72 on Japanese tourist-trade organization
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a report on organizing Japan’s tourist trade on an industrial basis and creating a control body in the Railway Department.
subfiles.summary: Filing sheet for Voluntary Report No. 72 on Japanese tourist-trade organization; the report is attached.

subfiles.title: Organization of Japanese Tourist Trade on an Industrial Basis and Creation of Control Organization in Department of Railways
subfiles.from: Leo D. Sturgeon, American Consul, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The report examines Japan’s coordinated governmental and commercial campaign to develop foreign tourism as part of national economic policy.
subfiles.summary: Sturgeon connects tourism promotion with the Hamaguchi government’s efforts to improve Japan’s trade balance and describes the Japan Tourist Bureau, its overseas advertising, hotel cooperation, and invitations to American travel professionals. He explains the newly created Board and Commission of Tourist Industry within the Railway Department, including plans for hotel loans, guide regulation, national parks, advertising, and conservation. The report concludes with observations and tables on tourist numbers and expenditures during the 1920s.

subfiles.title: Telegram advising Kate A. Forster about Chinese and Japanese visas in Seattle
subfiles.from: Ruth B. Shipley, Chief, Passport Division
subfiles.about: The Department states that Chinese and Japanese consular officers in Seattle can issue the required visas.
subfiles.summary: Reply to Kate Forster: Chinese and Japanese consular representation is available in Seattle for visas.

subfiles.title: Telegram asking whether Chinese and Japanese visas can be secured in Seattle
subfiles.about: Forster asks the Department to wire collect whether Chinese and Japanese visas are obtainable in Seattle.
subfiles.summary: Telegram asking whether Chinese and Japanese visas can be obtained in Seattle; it produced the reply on page 18.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for letter to Paul M. Overholtzer on entry documents for Japan
subfiles.about: The referenced letter states that a visaed regular American passport is the only credential ordinarily required for entry into Japan or Japanese-mandated territory.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a letter to Paul Overholtzer on Japanese entry-document requirements; the full letter is elsewhere.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Dollar Steamship Company representatives about an internment rumor
subfiles.about: Dollar Steamship representatives seek help countering a rumor that Chinese passengers bound for China were being interned at Japanese ports.
subfiles.summary: Dollar Steamship Company says an unfounded internment rumor discourages Chinese bookings and asks for a press statement; the Department declined and suggested approaching the Chinese Legation and Japanese Embassy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Charles Waterman’s letter concerning K. Chik Han
subfiles.about: The referenced letter concerns a Korean missionary wishing to travel through Japan to his home and family in Korea without detention.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Charles Waterman's letter about K. Chik Han, calling possible Japanese detention a wartime precaution.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Dard Hunter’s visa inquiry
subfiles.about: Hunter asks what procedure is necessary to obtain visas for travel in China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Dard Hunter's visa inquiry letter, filed under his name.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for protest over Langston Hughes’s detention in Japan
subfiles.from: National Committee for the Defense of Political Prisoners, associated with Ward
subfiles.about: The committee protests the allegedly unlawful detention of Langston Hughes after he entered Japan with approved passports and visas.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a protest over Langston Hughes's detention in Japan; his documents had been fully approved beforehand.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on Julian Street as a pro-Japanese writer
subfiles.about: The note considers including Julian Street among pro-Japanese writers and recalls his earlier favorable book about Japan.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten note calls Julian Street's earlier writing thoroughly pro-Japanese, its only oddity an extended praise of the Japanese bathhouse.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 590: Pro-Japanese Writers
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew reports that Japan’s International Tourist Bureau planned to fund another visit by author Julian Street.
subfiles.summary: The Railway Ministry’s tourist bureau reportedly appropriated ¥10,000 to bring Street back to Japan. Officials hoped the author of Mysterious Japan would write another story capable of attracting foreign tourists.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 9282: Issuance of Japanese Visas to Officers of American Armed Forces
subfiles.from: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Cunningham reports that the Japanese consulate will stop placing visas on military travel orders and will require passports or detailed nationality certificates.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 9282: the Japanese consul general ended visas on travel orders for American armed forces officers; Cunningham had urged using passports and copied the Legation and Marine and Fleet commanders.

subfiles.title: Itaro Ishii’s notice ending visas on American military travel orders
subfiles.from: Itaro Ishii, Japanese Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.to: Edwin S. Cunningham, American Consul General, Shanghai
subfiles.about: Ishii announces that Japanese visas will henceforth be placed only on regular passports or suitably detailed certificates of nationality.
subfiles.summary: Itaro Ishii's notice: the Home Office says visaing American naval travel orders breaches regulations; substitute nationality certificates need photographs and personal, service and travel details.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for the Frederic N. Pugsley visa-fee complaint
subfiles.about: The referenced letter reports that the Japanese consul at San Francisco demanded a ten-dollar visa fee from Pugsley, his wife, and his daughter for a visit of under seven days.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Lt. Cdr. Frederic Pugsley's complaint that a visa fee was charged separately for all three family members.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Curtis Vinson’s Japanese-visa inquiry
subfiles.about: Vinson asks for the address to which he should forward his American passport to obtain a Japanese visa.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Curtis Vinson's routine Japanese visa inquiry, filed under his name.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 749 on the Marcus Show
subfiles.about: The despatch concerns difficulties faced by an American revue troupe whose members received only one-month transit visas.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 749: the Marcus Show's treatment compared with free visas for Japanese entertainers under the 1926 arrangement, a reciprocity question.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for report on J. W. B. Smith’s refusal of permission to land
subfiles.about: Smith was refused permission to land at Yokohama because he lacked a passport despite carrying an appointment letter for special duty in the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a report on J. W. B. Smith's refusal of permission to land: his Assistant Attorney General letter was not accepted as a travel document.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Report No. 145 on foreign entertainers in Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a detailed report on Japanese rules governing the temporary admission, residence, and employment of foreign performers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Report No. 145 on foreign entertainers in Japan, citing the Kaili troupe's eviction.

subfiles.title: Report No. 145: Conditions of Temporary Admission and Residence of Instrumental Musicians, Other Musicians, Actors, Artists, and Choristers
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: The report explains the laws and administrative practices applied to foreign entertainers entering and working in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allison finds no special statute for performers, but explains that general alien-entry rules were enforced against them more strictly than against ordinary tourists or business travelers. Local guarantees were commonly demanded, practices varied among police authorities, and transit visas were used to limit stays. The Kaili troupe’s passport seizure, employment in Tokyo, and eventual expulsion demonstrate the arbitrary application of these rules; the report also links opposition to foreign performers with local commercial competition.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Report No. 146 on other alien workers
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies a report on temporary admission for alien employment outside the entertainer categories covered in Report No. 145.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Report No. 146 on other alien workers, answering the September 14, 1934 circular and referring to Report No. 145.

subfiles.title: Report No. 146: Conditions of Temporary Admission and Residence of Aliens for Employment Other Than Specified in Report No. 145
subfiles.from: J. M. Allison, American Vice Consul
subfiles.about: The report states that Japan had no special regulations for temporary alien workers beyond the general employment and entry rules already reported.
subfiles.summary: Allison refers the Department to Vice Consul Hutchinson’s November 1932 study for full details. He reports that no changes had occurred in the applicable regulations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 305 on Peter J. Ringens’s visa fee
subfiles.about: The despatch reports that the Japanese consulate at Singapore charged Peter J. Ringens a visa fee despite the U.S.-Japanese agreement.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 305: Peter Ringens, holding a service passport, was charged a visa fee that violated the US-Japan treaty arrangement.

subfiles.title: Passport Division recommendation concerning naval officers going ashore in Japan
subfiles.about: The note recommends action to ensure that naval officers going ashore in Japan carry valid passports visaed by Japanese consular officers.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten recommendation supports the request prompted by the Kobe consul’s report. It emphasizes advance compliance with Japanese passport and visa requirements for naval personnel.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 515: Passports for U.S. Naval Officers in Transit Through Japan
subfiles.about: Donovan urges the Navy Department to warn officers that passports with Japanese visas are required even for brief shore visits.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 515: two of ten naval officers on the President Adams lacked documents and were refused landing at Kobe until exceptional permission; Navy orders are not recognized as travel documents.

subfiles.title: State Department note requesting passport guidance for naval officers
subfiles.about: The State Department asks the Navy to ensure that officers intending to land in Japan possess valid passports with Japanese visas.
subfiles.summary: State note requests passport guidance for naval officers, enclosing the Kobe consul's July 27 despatch and listing passport-issuing authorities.

subfiles.title: Navy Department acknowledgment of passport requirements
subfiles.from: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The Navy acknowledges the Kobe despatch and promises to inform naval personnel about passport requirements at foreign ports.
subfiles.summary: The Navy acknowledges the passport requirements for officers landing in Japan and will advise naval personnel.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Millard Caldwell’s complaint about treatment of U.S. visitors
subfiles.about: Caldwell contrasts Japan’s treatment of American visitors with the access allegedly given Japanese nationals and other foreigners in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Millard Caldwell's complaint that visitors in the US got preferential access to secret information and inventions and permission to photograph topography.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 271 on passengers aboard USS Gold Star
subfiles.about: The despatch concerns Japanese passport requirements for passengers traveling aboard the naval supply ship Gold Star to Guam.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 271: Japan will not let USS Gold Star passengers land on Guam certificates without a consulate guarantee; the consul advises Navy passports.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 305 on Ralph and Mrs. Caples
subfiles.about: The despatch records the admission of Ralph and Mrs. Caples into Japan despite their lack of Japanese visas.
subfiles.summary: The steamship company arranged the couple’s admission with Japanese authorities. Consequently, the American consulate did not need to intervene.

subfiles.title: Letter on reentry into Taiwan by Chinese employees traveling abroad
subfiles.about: The writer reports that Chinese residents leaving Taiwan for destinations outside the Japanese Empire would not be readmitted during the China Incident.
subfiles.summary: Coughlin sought assurance two Chinese employees could travel to China and return to Taiwan; Japan barred reentry unless the consul guaranteed silence on the conflict, so they abandoned the trip.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Hornbeck on possible discrimination against German Jews
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes evidence of a Japanese-German understanding restricting travel to Japan by German nationals of Jewish faith.
subfiles.summary: Memo for Hornbeck: German Jewish travelers apparently needed prior Japanese permission before German passports valid for Japan were issued, raising possible exclusion of new arrivals.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 383: Possible Discriminatory Treatment of German Nationals of Jewish Faith
subfiles.from: C. R. Cameron, American Consul General, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Cameron reports indications that German Jews needed prior Japanese permission before receiving passports valid for travel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 383: Japanese water police control entry; a German Jewish resident needed permits for his parents and another similar application was refused, so assurances do not preclude excluding new Jews.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 421 on new Japanese immigration regulations
subfiles.about: The sheet records a despatch announcing new Japanese government regulations concerning immigration.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 421 on new Japanese immigration regulations governing residence, trade and travel.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3825: Aliens’ Entry, Sojourn and Departure
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits a published English translation of Japan’s new regulations governing aliens.
subfiles.summary: The regulations were scheduled to take effect on May 1, 1939, but the Embassy did not yet know how they would be administered in practice. Grew encloses W. J. Sebald’s translation, published by the Japan Chronicle Press in Kobe.

subfiles.title: In Re the Entry, Sojourn, & Departure of Aliens: Home Affairs Ordinance No. 6 of 1939
subfiles.from: Japanese Department of Home Affairs, translated by W. J. Sebald
subfiles.about: The ordinance establishes comprehensive rules for alien entry, transit, residence reporting, documentation, fees, departure, and deportation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The law distinguishes entry from transit, requires passports and Japanese visas subject to reciprocity, authorizes special permits, and limits transit stays to fifteen days. It imposes hotel reporting, alien-residence registration, police-document inspection, and advance departure-notification requirements. It also creates travel certificates for China and Manchukuo, establishes fees and penalties, defines grounds for deportation, and repeals the 1918 ordinance effective May 1, 1939.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Japanese Embassy note transmitting alien-entry regulations
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges receipt of the Japanese Embassy’s note and the enclosed English translations of the new alien-entry measures.
subfiles.summary: Acknowledges Japanese Embassy Note No. 106 of May 11, 1939 and thanks the ambassador for the Home Department ordinance and explanatory revision.

subfiles.title: Memorandum recommending acknowledgment of the Japanese Embassy communication
subfiles.about: The memorandum recommends acknowledging the Japanese Embassy’s transmission without taking further action.
subfiles.summary: Memo recommends acknowledging the Embassy's communication, since the Tokyo consulate general already sent the regulations and other departments are unlikely to be interested.

subfiles.title: Visa Division memorandum on fees under the 1939 Japanese ordinance
subfiles.about: The memorandum concludes that fees under the new ordinance do not violate the 1926 U.S.-Japanese visa-fee agreement.
subfiles.summary: Visa Division: fees were waived only for temporary visitors; other charges applied to special entry, transit, residence or departure, so no objection.

subfiles.title: Japanese Embassy Note No. 106 transmitting revised alien-entry regulations
subfiles.about: The ambassador transmits English-language copies of the new Home Department ordinance and an explanation of its revision.
subfiles.summary: Japanese Embassy Note No. 106 transmits revised alien-entry regulations from the Japanese Foreign Office for forwarding to US authorities.

subfiles.title: Revision of the Ordinance Concerning the Entry of Foreigners
subfiles.from: Japanese Foreign Office or Home Department
subfiles.about: The enclosure explains the reasons for and principal innovations in Japan’s revised 1939 foreigner-entry ordinance.
subfiles.summary: The document says the 1918 ordinance had become inadequate and that the revision was intended to improve the control and protection of foreigners in Japan Proper. It explains the new fifteen-day distinction between entry and transit and formalizes special entry and transit permits for travelers lacking ordinary passports or visas. The surviving pages also justify ¥20 and ¥10 permit fees and begin discussing the new system of permission for sojourn; the document continues beyond page 80.
